claims.text: Since October 14, 2024, San Francisco's Rent Ordinance § 37.10C has prohibited selling or using algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy for residential units. These are software tools that analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents for vacant units. A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action if they believe an entity is violating the law.

New law prohibits algorithmic devices used to set rents in San Francisco | SF.gov

news
New law prohibits algorithmic devices used to set rents in San Francisco
Rent Board
New law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
October 16, 2024
Legislation
adding Section 37.10C to the Rent Ordinance went into effect on October 14, 2024. The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
The term “algorithmic device” means a device such as a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purposes of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit. The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.

claims.text: Under Hoboken City Code § 158-2 (Article II, adopted 7-9-2025 by Ord. No. B-781), landlords who rent a residential dwelling unit in Hoboken may not engage in "price fixing using algorithmic pricing." A residential dwelling unit means any primary residence, excluding medical/long-term care and detention facilities, so not every rental property is covered. The ban covers using software, algorithms, or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information from other real estate lessors in order to coordinate, recommend, or implement rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels among competing lessors. Nonpublic competitor information is information such as prices, supply levels, security deposits, ideal occupancy levels, lease termination and renewal dates, or other material terms that is less than 365 days old and not widely and readily available to the public at no cost; older or freely available information is outside that definition. The Division of Housing or an aggrieved private citizen may bring alleged violations in Hoboken Municipal Court. On conviction, penalties are one or more of: penalties under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5, a fine up to $2,000, or community service up to 90 days. The supplied evidence does not state a separate effective date.

A service provider is a person that performs a coordination function for a real estate lessor or rentor: collecting nonpublic competitor information, analyzing or processing it with computational tools, and recommending rental prices, lease terms, or occupancy levels. The coordination definition exempts owners of multiple properties for actions related exclusively to properties controlled by the same rental property owner, and licensed real estate agents operating in accordance with state regulations are not included as service providers. Residential dwelling units are units intended as a person's primary residence, excluding inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. The supplied evidence gives no exact effective date.

claims.text: In Jersey City, it is unlawful for a real estate lessor, an agent, or a subcontractor of either to subscribe to, contract with, exchange anything of value for, or otherwise use the services of a "Service Provider." A Service Provider is any person who performs a "coordination" function for a lessor. Coordination means collecting nonpublic competitor information from lessors (plus historical or current prices, supply levels, occupancy rates, or lease termination and renewal dates from two or more lessors or from public databases), processing it with a system or software that uses computation, and recommending rents, lease terms, or occupancy levels to a lessor. The definition does not cover owners of multiple properties acting only on properties controlled by the same owner, and it does not cover licensed real estate agents who are operating in accordance with applicable state regulations. The rules also apply only to "residential dwelling units," meaning units intended as a person's primary residence, and they exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. A separate provision says no service provider may facilitate an agreement not to compete among lessors on rental pricing, fees, or other rental terms.

claims.text: Under California's new Business and Professions Code section 16729, subsection (b) makes it unlawful for a person to use or distribute a "common pricing algorithm" if that person coerces another person to set or adopt a price or commercial term the algorithm recommends for the same or similar products or services in California. A common pricing algorithm is any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. "Distribute" includes selling, licensing, providing access to, or otherwise making available, including by subscription. A "person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service. Coercion is not the only way to violate the section. Subsection (a) separately makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade. This is a general rule about common pricing algorithms, not a rental-specific ban.

claims.text: In Hoboken, a residential landlord who wants to raise a current tenant's rent by more than 10% year over year when renewing the lease must make four disclosures to the tenant before the increase is implemented. The disclosures go either in the renewal lease, clearly indicated on its first page, or on a form provided by the Hoboken Division of Housing. They are: (1) an itemization of the costs associated with the increase; (2) a statement whether a rent algorithm was used to set it; (3) a statement that the tenant may take legal action, at their own expense, if they believe the increase is unconscionable or otherwise not in accordance with local or state law; and (4) the Division of Housing's contact information, with a statement that tenants may reach out to the Division and/or the Tenant Advocate with questions or concerns. A landlord who pleads guilty to or is found guilty of failing to provide these disclosures can be fined up to $1,000 per incident. This rule is about disclosures for increases over 10%, not a cap on rent increases.
